items.title: Decline is not the end — vinyl records came back
items.claim: Vinyl record sales collapsed from the mid-1980s as CDs took over. What has happened since the late 2000s?

options.text: Vinyl sales have risen every year from 2007 to 2023, overtaking CDs in US revenue terms in 2022 for the first time since 1987 (RIAA data)

items.reveal:
RIAA US data: vinyl revenue fell to under $20m by 2006. By 2022, vinyl revenue was $1.2bn — overtaking CDs ($483m) for the first time in 35 years. UK Official Charts data shows similar pattern from 2008 onwards.

The textbook PLC implies decline is terminal. Brand repositioning, nostalgia and physical-product premiums in a streaming world reversed that trajectory. Other examples: Polaroid film, Kodak Super 8, mechanical watches.
items.why: The four-stage product life cycle is a framework, not a law of nature. Decline can be reversed by changing what the product means to customers.

items.title: Maslow's pyramid was never drawn by Maslow
items.claim: Maslow's Hierarchy of Needs is taught with a pyramid. What did Maslow himself draw?

options.text: He drew the pyramid himself in his 1943 paper
He never drew it as a pyramid; the pyramid representation was introduced by management consultants and textbooks in the 1960s
He drew it as a circle to indicate non-linear progression
He explicitly rejected any visual representation

items.reveal:
Todd Bridgman, Stephen Cummings and John Ballard's 2019 paper in the Academy of Management Learning & Education traced the pyramid to Charles McDermid's 1960 management article in Business Horizons. Maslow's 1943 'A Theory of Human Motivation' described needs as overlapping and dynamic — not rigidly tiered.

Maslow himself, late in his career, qualified the theory heavily: needs can be pursued in parallel, prioritisation varies by culture and individual, and self-actualisation isn't a 'top' level so much as a developmental orientation.

Empirical tests find weak support for the strict hierarchy.
items.why: The most-taught motivation diagram in business education was drawn by someone other than the named theorist and oversimplifies what he wrote. Worth checking what's in the textbook against what's in the source.

items.title: Ansoff said diversification was the riskiest growth strategy
items.claim: Igor Ansoff's 1957 'Strategies for Diversification' in Harvard Business Review introduced a 2x2 matrix. Which growth strategy did he flag as carrying highest risk?

options.text: Diversification (new product, new market) — combining product and market uncertainty multiplies risk

items.reveal:
Ansoff's matrix sequences risk: market penetration (existing product, existing market) is safest; product development and market development each add one source of uncertainty; diversification adds two.

Empirical work (Markides 1995, McKinsey 2010s) has supported this in aggregate: unrelated diversification destroys shareholder value more often than not. The 1960s conglomerate boom (ITT, Hanson) and its 1990s breakup vindicated Ansoff's warning.
items.why: Growth strategies look attractive on the upside; Ansoff's matrix forces you to articulate the downside risks for each route.
